newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian '97 GDP growth seen slower at 4.9 pct.
newsitem.headline: Croatian '97 GDP growth seen slower at 4.9 pct.

text.p: Croatia's 1997 real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth may reach 4.9 percent with an inflation rate of 4.6 percent, leading commercial bank Zagrebacka Banka said on Monday in an independent forecast.
This year's growth forecast was cut down from an earlier 5.5 percent after a decline in the fourth quarter of 1996, caused by what the bank described as "weakening of the industrial activity".
"Thus the growing trend recorded in the first three quarters of 1996 was almost brought to an end," Zagrebacka's chief economist Zarko Miljenovic said in a quarterly forecast.
He trimmed last year's GDP growth estimate to only 3.7 percent, compared to 5-7 percent seen by the government.
Construction, trade and tourism performed well, but a slower than expected growth in public expenditure was said to have been another negative factor.
The industrial output, representing roughly one third of GDP, rose 3.1 percent. The 1997 rise is seen at 3.7 percent.
But despite the setback in the last quarter, a relative upward trend was preserved and may be carried over into this year, Miljenovic said.
"In 1997, major inducements to growth are expected to come again from personal and investment consumption," he added, also anticipating an 11-percent increase in exports.
Stronger export demand, coupled with a gradual recovery of domestic demand, would in turn spur production of capital goods which has stagnated since mid-1996.
Due to wage increases and tax cuts, disposable personal incomes and household consumption were seen as rising 12 percent, partly stimulated by stronger lending by local banks.
Domestic investment demand was seen as growing steadily thanks to reconstruction and road building efforts, and a continued modernisation of Croatian companies.
However, it was also expected to lead to a 17-percent imports rise, particularly of capital goods, thus allowing the trade deficit to widen to $3.7 billion this year from $3.3 billion in 1996.
"The expected acceleration of domestic business cycle in 1997 will be reflected in somewhat higher inflation rate," Miljenovic said.
His annual retail price inflation forecast of 4.6 percent compares to 3.5 percent in 1996, and is outside the 3-4 percent target for this year given by the central bank.
Miljenovic upped the 1997 figure for inflation at the factory gate to 2.7 from an earlier 2.1 percent, and only 1.3 percent recorded last year. -- Kolumbina Bencevic, Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075
